youtube.title: Boeing's $13 Billion McDonnell Douglas Deal, 22 Years Before the MAX
youtube.description:
In December 1996 Boeing agreed to buy a struggling rival, McDonnell Douglas, for $13.3 billion. Twenty-two years later, two 737 MAX crashes killed 346 people and the plane was grounded worldwide. How did one merger and the choices that followed it lead there, and is the popular story the whole story?

This documentary follows the record: the 1996 deal papers, the 2000 engineers' strike, the move to Chicago, the 2011 decision to re-engine the 737 instead of designing a new jet, the congressional findings, and where the money and the company ended up.

{CHAPTERS}

youtube.comment: Should Boeing have designed a new jet in 2011 instead of the 737 MAX? 👇

sources.claim: On 13 March 2019 the US grounded every Boeing 737 MAX
sources.source: FAA Emergency Order of Prohibition, 13 March 2019

sources.claim: Two crashes in under five months killed 346 people
sources.source: KNKT final report on Lion Air 610 (Oct 2019, 189 dead); Ethiopian AIB final report on ET302 (Dec 2022, 157 dead)

sources.claim: Boeing agreed to buy McDonnell Douglas for $13.3 billion on 15 December 1996, in an all-stock deal of 0.65 Boeing shares per McDonnell Douglas share
sources.source: Boeing/McDonnell Douglas joint announcement, 15 Dec 1996; The New York Times, 16 Dec 1996

sources.claim: Seattle joke: McDonnell Douglas bought Boeing with Boeing's money
sources.source: Peter Robison, Flying Blind (Doubleday, 2021); The Seattle Times reporting

sources.claim: The MAX crashes were not the result of a singular failure, technical mistake, or mismanaged event
sources.source: US House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, Final Committee Report on the Boeing 737 MAX, 16 Sept 2020

sources.claim: The 777 entered service with United Airlines on 7 June 1995
sources.source: Boeing 777 history, Boeing.com; United Airlines, June 1995

sources.claim: The 777 was designed on computers in three dimensions instead of paper drawings
sources.source: Boeing 777 history, Boeing.com; Karl Sabbagh, 21st-Century Jet (1996)

sources.claim: Engineers from eight airlines sat inside the 777 design teams
sources.source: Boeing 'Working Together' programme, Boeing.com; Sabbagh, 21st-Century Jet (1996)

sources.claim: The 777 was approved for 180-minute ETOPS on 30 May 1995, before its first passenger flight
sources.source: FAA type certificate and ETOPS approval, 30 May 1995; Boeing.com 777 history

sources.claim: Boeing's 1996 sales were $22.7 billion
sources.source: Boeing 1996 Annual Report

sources.claim: Boeing's chairman was an engineer who helped lead the 777 programme
sources.source: Boeing executive biography of Philip M. Condit, 1996

sources.claim: McDonnell Douglas airliners were losing ground to Boeing and Airbus
sources.source: The New York Times, 16 Dec 1996

sources.claim: McDonnell Douglas shelved the MD-XX in October 1996
sources.source: McDonnell Douglas announcement, Oct 1996; Flight International, Nov 1996

sources.claim: On 16 November 1996 the Pentagon picked Boeing and Lockheed Martin for the Joint Strike Fighter contest, leaving McDonnell Douglas out
sources.source: US Department of Defense announcement, 16 Nov 1996

sources.claim: That contest produced the F-35
sources.source: US Department of Defense, award to Lockheed Martin, 26 Oct 2001

sources.claim: In 1993 the deputy defence secretary told industry chiefs the budget could not keep them all; one chief executive called it the Last Supper
sources.source: Norman Augustine, accounts in Augustine's Laws (6th ed., 1997) and interviews; William Perry's recollections, 1993 dinner

sources.claim: In 1996 Boeing bought Rockwell's aerospace and defence business for $3.2 billion
sources.source: Boeing announcement, 1 Aug 1996

sources.claim: McDonnell Douglas made fighters and the C-17 cargo jet
sources.source: McDonnell Douglas 1996 Annual Report

sources.claim: Harry Stonecipher became Boeing's president after the merger
sources.source: Boeing/McDonnell Douglas joint announcement, 15 Dec 1996

sources.claim: On 23 July 1997 the European Commission cleared the deal after Boeing gave up exclusive 20-year supply deals with American, Delta and Continental
sources.source: European Commission Decision 97/816/EC, July 1997

sources.claim: The merger closed on 1 August 1997, making Boeing the world's largest aerospace company
sources.source: Boeing announcement, 1 Aug 1997

sources.claim: In October 1997 Boeing halted its 747 and 737 lines for about a month
sources.source: Boeing announcement, Oct 1997; The Seattle Times, Oct 1997

sources.claim: Boeing posted a $178 million net loss for 1997, its first loss in about half a century
sources.source: Boeing 1997 Annual Report; The New York Times, Jan 1998

sources.claim: Boeing blamed production problems for the 1997 loss
sources.source: Boeing 1997 Annual Report

sources.claim: In February 2000 about 17,000 engineers and technical workers struck for 40 days, described as the largest white-collar strike in US history
sources.source: SPEEA records; The Seattle Times, Feb-Mar 2000

sources.claim: In 2001 Boeing moved its head office from Seattle to Chicago, about 2,800 km away; Boeing said headquarters should be separate from any one business unit
sources.source: Boeing announcements, 21 March and 10 May 2001

sources.claim: Stonecipher became chief executive in December 2003
sources.source: Boeing announcement, 1 Dec 2003

sources.claim: "When people say I changed the culture of Boeing, that was the intent, so that it's run like a business rather than a great engineering firm."
sources.source: Harry Stonecipher, interview, Chicago Tribune, 2004

sources.claim: In June 2005 Boeing sold its Wichita plant, which became Spirit AeroSystems
sources.source: Boeing announcement, June 2005; Spirit AeroSystems S-1 filing, 2006

sources.claim: 787 sections were built by suppliers in Japan, Italy and the US
sources.source: Boeing 787 programme fact sheets, 2007

sources.claim: The 787 first flew on 15 December 2009, more than two years late; first delivery came in September 2011, more than three years late
sources.source: Boeing announcements, 15 Dec 2009 and 26 Sept 2011

sources.claim: On 20 July 2011 American Airlines ordered 460 jets, 260 from Airbus, half of them A320neos
sources.source: AMR Corporation announcement, 20 July 2011

sources.claim: Boeing launched the 737 MAX on 30 August 2011
sources.source: Boeing press release, 'Boeing Launches 737 New Engine Family with Commitments for 496 Airplanes from Five Airlines', 30 Aug 2011

sources.claim: The 737 first flew in 1967
sources.source: Boeing 737 history, Boeing.com

sources.claim: Bigger engines sat further forward and higher, changing pitch behaviour; Boeing added MCAS to push the nose down
sources.source: US House T&I Committee final report, 16 Sept 2020

sources.claim: Boeing promised Southwest $1 million per plane if MAX pilots needed simulator training
sources.source: US House T&I Committee final report, 16 Sept 2020

sources.claim: MCAS was not described in the pilots' operating manual
sources.source: US House T&I Committee final report, 16 Sept 2020

sources.claim: "This airplane is designed by clowns who in turn are supervised by monkeys."
sources.source: Boeing internal messages released to Congress, published 9 Jan 2020

sources.claim: Lion Air 610 crashed into the Java Sea about 13 minutes after take-off on 29 Oct 2018; all 189 aboard died
sources.source: KNKT final report, 25 Oct 2019

sources.claim: One faulty sensor fed MCAS bad data repeatedly
sources.source: KNKT final report, 25 Oct 2019

sources.claim: The FAA issued an emergency directive to MAX crews on 7 Nov 2018 and the MAX kept flying
sources.source: FAA Emergency Airworthiness Directive 2018-23-51, 7 Nov 2018

sources.claim: Ethiopian 302 crashed about six minutes after leaving Addis Ababa on 10 March 2019; all 157 aboard died
sources.source: Ethiopian AIB final report, Dec 2022

sources.claim: China grounded the MAX on 11 March 2019; the US followed on 13 March
sources.source: CAAC notice, 11 March 2019; FAA order, 13 March 2019
Boeing Form 10-K annual reports, 2018-2024

sources.claim: 2019's $636 million loss was Boeing's first annual loss since 1997
sources.source: Boeing Q4 2019 results, 29 Jan 2020; Reuters, 29 Jan 2020

sources.claim: Boeing's chief executive was removed on 23 Dec 2019
sources.source: Boeing announcement, 23 Dec 2019

sources.claim: The House report blamed faulty engineering assumptions, management's lack of transparency and grossly insufficient FAA oversight
sources.source: US House T&I Committee final report, 16 Sept 2020

sources.claim: The FAA cleared the MAX on 18 Nov 2020
sources.source: FAA rescission order, 18 Nov 2020

sources.claim: Boeing agreed to pay $2.5 billion, including a $500 million fund for crash victims' families, over a charge of conspiracy to defraud the FAA
sources.source: US Department of Justice press release, 7 Jan 2021

sources.claim: Boeing agreed to plead guilty in July 2024; a federal judge rejected the deal in December 2024
sources.source: DOJ court filing, July 2024; US District Court, N.D. Texas, order of 5 Dec 2024

sources.claim: In May 2025 the Justice Department moved to drop the charge; many families objected
sources.source: DOJ announcement, May 2025; families' filings and statements reported by Reuters, May 2025

sources.claim: In 2019 Airbus delivered 863 jets, Boeing 380
sources.source: Airbus and Boeing annual delivery figures, Jan 2020

sources.claim: On 5 Jan 2024 a door plug blew out of an Alaska Airlines MAX 9 at about 16,000 feet; no one died
sources.source: NTSB preliminary report, 6 Feb 2024

sources.claim: The four bolts meant to hold the door plug had not been reinstalled
sources.source: NTSB preliminary report, 6 Feb 2024

sources.claim: In July 2024 Boeing agreed to buy back Spirit AeroSystems
sources.source: Boeing announcement, 1 July 2024

sources.claim: In August 2024 an engineer who once ran Rockwell Collins became Boeing's chief executive
sources.source: Boeing announcement, 31 July 2024 (effective 8 Aug 2024)

sources.claim: Boeing spent about $43 billion buying back its own shares, 2013-2019
sources.source: Boeing Form 10-K annual reports, 2013-2019

sources.claim: The grounding's direct costs passed $20 billion
sources.source: Boeing disclosures as totalled by Reuters, 18 Nov 2020

sources.claim: Kodak built the first digital camera in 1975
sources.source: Kodak corporate history; US Patent 4,131,919 (1978)
